A write-ahead log is a sequence of records that a database writes to persistent storage before writing data to its main storage. This ensures that all transactions are safely written to disk in a specific order.
If a crash occurs, the database can recover by replaying the log from the point of the crash. This means that the database can reapply any transactions that were not yet written to main storage.
The write-ahead log is essential for maintaining consistency and integrity of the database. By replaying the log, the database ensures that all transactions are applied correctly, even if some were partially written before the crash. This prevents lost or corrupted data.
By using a write-ahead log, a database can recover from crashes without significant data loss or corruption. The database can then continue operating as if the crash had never happened.
Example Use Case: A financial database stores transactions in its main storage. If a crash occurs during a transaction, the database can recover by replaying the write-ahead log. The database write-ahead log works by writing each transaction to the log before actually writing it to the primary database. A write-ahead log is a database that writes changes to a file called a journal before it actually makes those changes to the main database. This is done to provide a record of changes that have been made, but not yet written to the main database. The key idea behind this approach is that the database can recover after a crash by replaying the changes recorded in the journal. If the database crashes while it is in the middle of a transaction, the changes that have already been written to the journal are still safe, even if they haven't been written to the main database. Here are a few key steps that the database would follow in order to recover.

## Step 1: Identify the last checkpoint
The database identifies the last checkpoint, which is the most recent point at which all data was safely written to disk. This ensures that any changes made after the last checkpoint can be safely discarded.

## Step 2: Replay the journal
The database replays the journal, applying the changes recorded in the journal to the main database from the last checkpoint onwards. This brings the database up to date with the changes that were made before the crash.
